svg.aria-label: Diagram comparing an appliance failure in a Gateway Load Balancer inspection path before and after TCP Reset. On the left, before: the appliance fails its health check, the existing flow stays pinned to it because target_failover.on_unhealthy defaults to no_rebalance, packets are dropped silently, and the client retransmits until its own TCP stack times out, which AWS describes as several minutes. On the right, after: with TCP Reset enabled on the target group, Gateway Load Balancer sends a reset packet, the client learns immediately, and the client opens a new connection which is placed on a healthy appliance. A band across the bottom records that the flow itself is still not rebalanced, that recovery happens because the client reconnects, and that the same reset is sent on deregistration and on idle timeout expiry.
svg.title: TCP Reset for Gateway Load Balancer changes who knows the flow is dead, not where the flow goes
svg.text: The flow does not move. The client is simply told.

Enabled per target group. No charge.
The flow is still not rebalanced. Recovery happens because the client reconnects. The same reset is
also sent on deregistration — where the drain default is 300 seconds — and when a flow’s idle timeout expires.
Leaving no_rebalance in place is deliberate: a stateful appliance that never saw the handshake may drop a moved flow as out-of-state.
